findings.title: A backup code plus any arbitrary non-empty totpCode bypasses password verification
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() flow, the password check above (lines 121-129) only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`. The new backup-code branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` runs regardless of whether the password was ever verified. An attacker who knows a victim's email and one backup code (a static 10-hex-character secret, e.g. from the downloadable cal-backup-codes.txt) can log in by submitting email + backupCode + any dummy non-empty totpCode such as "000000": the presence of totpCode makes the password-verification condition false, and the backup-code branch then authenticates them and creates a session. Backup codes are intended as a second factor in addition to the password; this makes one static factor alone sufficient for account takeover. The skip exists to support the IdP totp redirect flow, but the backup-code branch should require successful password verification for CAL (password) users, or the password check should not be conditioned on totpCode being absent.

findings.title: onEnable only fires from the backup-codes Close button, leaving stale state on other dismiss paths
findings.body: Before this change, `onEnable()` (which makes the parent settings page refresh and show the 2FA switch as enabled) ran immediately when /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable returned 200. It is now replaced with `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and only called from the "Close" button on the backup-codes screen. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way — the dialog's X button, Escape key, or overlay click, all routed through `onOpenChange` — `onEnable()` never runs, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled even though it is now on (until a manual refetch), and `resetState()` also doesn't run, so reopening the modal lands on the stale backup-codes screen displaying the old codes. The parent notification/state reset should happen on any close of the final step, not just the Close button.

findings.title: Backup codes cannot be used by Google/SAML users in the IdP two-factor challenge
findings.body: When a Google/SAML user with 2FA signs in, they are redirected to /auth/login?totp=<jwt>, which renders the TOTP input with `ExternalTotpFooter` — only a Cancel button, no "Lost access" option — so there is no way in the UI to enter a backup code. A backup-code-only request is also rejected server-side: in next-auth-options.ts the guards `user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode` (lines 113-121) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled / IncorrectEmailPassword before the new backup-code branch is reached. Consequence: identity-provider users who lose their authenticator remain locked out despite having valid backup codes; the recovery feature only works for CAL password accounts.

findings.title: Consumed backup codes are nulled in place instead of removed
findings.body: After a successful backup-code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is persisted rather than splicing the used code out of the array. The stored JSON keeps accumulating null placeholders, `user.backupCodes` stays truthy forever, and once all 10 codes have been used the user gets `IncorrectBackupCode` instead of an indication that their codes are exhausted (`MissingBackupCodes` only fires when codes were never generated). Splice the redeemed code out and treat an empty array the same as having no backup codes.

findings.title: Backup-code verification and consumption are not atomic
findings.body: The authorize flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then issues a separate `prisma.user.update` to persist the remaining codes. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update commits, so a nominally single-use code can be redeemed twice within the race window. Consider consuming the code atomically (e.g., in a transaction with a re-read/optimistic check) or documenting acceptance of the risk.

findings.title: missing_backup_codes message instructs users to do something impossible
findings.body: The new string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown on the login page when a user with 2FA enabled but no backup codes uses the "Lost access" flow — i.e., users who enabled 2FA before this feature existed and are now locked out of their authenticator. There is no settings UI to (re)generate backup codes for an account that already has 2FA enabled (codes are only created during initial setup), and a locked-out user cannot reach settings anyway. The recovery instruction cannot be followed and will generate support tickets.

findings.title: First 2FA e2e test not updated for the new backup-code screen; its assertion is admittedly broken
findings.body: In "should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA", after the OTP is accepted the modal now displays the backup-codes screen, but the test never interacts with it or closes it (unlike the second test, which was updated). The subsequent check on the switch state is annotated with a newly added FIXME stating it passes even when the switch is not checked, and since `onEnable` now only fires from the backup-codes Close button, the enabled state is never confirmed. This test would stay green even if enabling 2FA regressed. It should close the backup-code screen and assert on `data-state="checked"` like the second test does.

findings.title: No test covers logging in with a backup code or its one-time-use guarantee
findings.body: The security-critical behavior introduced by this PR — authenticating with a backup code, rejecting an invalid code, and consuming a code so it cannot be reused — has no automated coverage. The added test code only checks the download filename and the copy toast, and a TODO acknowledges the missing tests. A regression making backup codes reusable, unconsumed, or rejected would ship undetected.

findings.title: navigator.clipboard used without an availability check
findings.body: The Copy button calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` directly. The Clipboard API is only exposed in secure contexts; on self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP, `navigator.clipboard` is undefined, so clicking Copy throws a TypeError and the user gets no feedback at all (the success toast is never reached). Feature-detect `navigator.clipboard` and fall back to a hidden-textarea copy, or show an error toast.
